section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
question: Beyond doing real work, what increasingly important roles do LLM agents play for the models being trained?
options: Generating their own training data, running their own experiments, and fixing their own code
Replacing the optimizer during pretraining by proposing per-step learning rates and momentum values
Compressing the trained model's weights for deployment by choosing which layers to quantize
Choosing tokenizer merges during BPE training so the vocabulary fits the target domain
explanation: Agents are how trained models get used, and increasingly how they produce training data, run experiments, and repair code. Research engineers both build agent scaffolds and act as the human debugging them.

section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
question: According to the view of agent engineering as a craft, what is the hard part of building an agent?
options: Writing the loop's control flow, which needs complex scheduling, threading, and state machines
Implementing tensor representations of the action space so the model can sample actions
Choosing the GPU type and batch size so the control loop runs at interactive latency
Getting the interface and the feedback right; the loop itself is simple
explanation: The loop is a few lines of control flow. Whether an agent works depends on the tool interface and on the feedback the observations provide.

section: 1. The causal story: one tool call is not enough
question: Why can't a task like 'fix the failing test in this repo' be planned entirely up front?
options: Each step depends on what the previous step revealed, such as a new failure after an edit
Repositories cannot be read by tools, so the agent has to guess file contents from the test name alone
Tests can only be run once per episode, so the plan must be finalized before the first test run
The model's context window forbids writing a multi-step plan before the first tool call is made
explanation: The task is a chain: inspect failure, find file, read code, edit, rerun, see a new failure, revise. You cannot write later actions before seeing earlier observations.

section: 1. The causal story: one tool call is not enough
question: What makes a tool-calling loop an agent?
options: A single tool call with a well-written JSON schema, so that the model's one request is always valid and parseable
A model larger than a fixed parameter threshold, above which multi-tool use becomes reliable enough to deploy
Running on a GPU cluster rather than one device, so that several tools can execute in parallel at every step
Many iterative actions with feedback (inspect, act, observe, correct), driven by a model reasoning about what to do next
explanation: A single call answers one question. Repeating inspect-act-observe-correct under a model's control is what defines an agent.

section: 1. The causal story: one tool call is not enough
question: On the ladder from plain LLM to agent, what distinguishes a tool-calling LLM from a ReAct agent?
options: A tool-calling LLM reasons in natural language but cannot act; ReAct acts on tools but never writes out its reasoning
A tool-calling LLM is trained with RL on tool rewards, while ReAct is trained only with SFT on human traces
A tool-calling LLM emits one structured call and reads one result; ReAct interleaves reasoning and acting in a loop
There is no real difference; the two terms are synonyms used by different labs for the same single-call setup
explanation: Module 18's tool-calling model handles a single call/result. ReAct adds the loop: think, act, observe, repeat.

section: 1. The causal story: one tool call is not enough
question: On the ladder from plain LLM to agent, what does the 'planning + iterative action' rung add beyond ReAct?
options: The agent stops calling tools and switches to reasoning only, having already gathered enough context
The agent's weights are updated by a gradient step after each observation so it learns within the task
The agent maintains a goal, breaks it into sub-steps, and adapts the plan as observations arrive
The agent runs several models in parallel and takes a majority vote over their proposed next actions
explanation: Planning adds explicit goal decomposition and plan revision on top of the think-act-observe loop. The full agent then wraps this with a task, tool interface, and stopping condition.

section: 1. The causal story: one tool call is not enough
question: What three things wrap the loop to make a complete agent on the ladder from plain LLM to agent?
options: A reward model, a value head, and a replay buffer
A tokenizer, an optimizer, and a learning-rate scheduler
A dataset, a validation split, and a held-out test split
A task, a tool interface, and a stopping condition
explanation: The agent rung is the whole loop wrapped with a task to solve, an interface of tools, and a condition for stopping.

question: In ReAct, what is a Thought?
options: A structured tool call with a tool name and JSON arguments that the loop executes immediately
The tool's return value, appended to the history so the model can condition on it at the next step
A hidden activation vector passed between steps that stores the model's plan outside the visible text
A short natural-language reasoning step the model generates about what it knows and what to do next
explanation: A Thought is just generated text, but it forces the model to plan in the open so the plan can condition the next action.

question: In ReAct, what is an Action?
options: A free-form sentence describing what the model intends to do next, written before any tool runs
A gradient update to the policy, applied after each step based on whether the tool call succeeded
A structured tool call (a tool name plus arguments) in the function-calling format
The final answer returned to the user once the loop decides that no further tool calls are needed
explanation: The Action follows the Module 18 function-calling format. The tool's result then becomes the Observation.

question: In ReAct, what is the Observation and what happens to it?
options: The model's own prediction of what the tool will return, used in place of actually running the tool
A human rating of the preceding action, stored as a scalar reward for later RL fine-tuning
A log entry recorded for debugging that is kept out of the model's context to save tokens
The tool's return value, fed back into the context so the next Thought can use it
explanation: Observations ground reasoning in real feedback. They are appended to the running history for the next step.

question: Why did Yao et al. find ReAct outperforms reasoning-only and acting-only approaches?
options: ReAct used a substantially larger model than all the baselines, so most of its gains simply reflect model scale
Reasoning picks good actions and actions ground reasoning in feedback; reasoning-only hallucinates, acting-only flails
ReAct never actually calls tools during evaluation, so it avoids all of the errors that real tool calls introduce
ReAct was fine-tuned on far more demonstration data than the acting-only methods it was compared against
explanation: Each component covers the other's weakness: reasoning without feedback makes things up, while acting without reasoning lacks direction.

question: When does a ReAct loop stop?
options: After exactly three Thought-Action-Observation cycles, regardless of progress
When the model emits a final answer instead of another action
As soon as any tool call returns an error string as its observation
When the newest Observation is identical to the previous Observation
explanation: ReAct repeats Thought, Action, Observation until a final answer appears. A step budget is a separate safety stop.

section: 2.1 Why a *deterministic* loop for a course
question: Why is an LLM policy unsuitable for teaching and unit-testing the ReAct mechanism?
options: It is non-deterministic and needs a GPU or API key, so runs aren't reproducible or testable
It cannot emit structured actions in the function-calling format, so the loop has nothing to parse
It is too accurate on toy tasks, so it routes around loop bugs and hides them from the tests
It requires tensors inside the loop, which forces the whole control flow to run on the GPU
explanation: Non-determinism and external dependencies make tests flaky and costly. A scripted policy makes every run reproducible.

section: 2.1 Why a *deterministic* loop for a course
question: How does the course's ReAct implementation separate concerns between loop and policy?
options: The loop contains the model and generates every thought; the policy is just the list of tools it may call
The loop is deterministic control flow; the policy is any callable policy(history) -> action, scripted in tests
The policy runs the tools and records their outputs, while the loop generates thoughts between tool calls
Both are merged into a single LLM call that returns the full trace and the final answer in one generation
explanation: The loop calls the policy, runs the named tool, appends the observation, and repeats. The policy decides actions. This is how real agent frameworks are structured.

section: 2.1 Why a *deterministic* loop for a course
question: Why is the course's deterministic ReAct agent honestly called a scaffold?
options: Because it cannot run any tools and only prints the actions it would have taken
Without a capable policy it only does what the script says
Because it has no step budget, so any policy that never finishes runs forever
Because it only works on GPUs, so it cannot be run in the course's CPU tests
explanation: The scripted policy lets you understand and test the plumbing, but it contains no intelligence. A real agent needs an LLM policy.

question: In the ReAct trace for computing (3 + 4) × 2 with add and mul tools, where did step 2's argument a=7 come from?
options: From step 1's observation, the result of add(3, 4)
From the task string, which the loop parses before step 1
From the policy computing the sum in advance, without a tool
From the mul tool's default argument, which is preset to 7
explanation: The dependency chain is the point: the second action could not be written before the first observation existed.

question: In the ReAct trace for (3 + 4) × 2, how does the policy signal completion?
options: By emitting the action {"final": 14} on step 3
By calling mul a second time with b=1 to signal no change
By returning an empty dict, which the loop reads as done
By raising StopIteration from inside the policy callable
explanation: The third step's action is {"final": 14}, and the loop stops, reporting finished after 3 steps with answer 14.

question: What does run_react do if max_steps is less than 1?
options: It raises ValueError
It runs exactly one step
It runs until the policy finalizes
It returns answer=None immediately
explanation: The guard raises ValueError(f"max_steps must be >= 1, got {max_steps}") before any loop iterations.

question: How does run_react give the policy access to the task?
options: It passes the task as a separate keyword argument on every single policy call
It stores the task in a module-level global variable the policy reads
It appends the task string to every tool's arguments before each call
It seeds history with a synthetic step 0 whose observation is the task
explanation: history[0] = Step(thought="task", action={"task": task}, observation=task), so the policy reads its goal from history like any other step. No special task channel is needed.

question: In run_react, how does the loop detect that the policy is done?
options: The action's tool name is the reserved string "stop"
The observation returned for the step is None
The thought text contains the keyword 'done' or 'finished'
The action dict contains a "final" key
explanation: If "final" in action, the loop appends the step with observation None and returns ReActResult with answer=action["final"] and finished=True.

question: In run_react, what observation results when the policy names a tool not in the tools dict?
options: A KeyError that ends the episode
The string "error: unknown tool '<name>'"
None, and the step is skipped
The loop calls the first available tool instead
explanation: Unknown tools produce an error string as the observation, which the policy can read and recover from next step.

question: In run_react, what happens when a tool raises an exception?
options: The exception propagates out of run_react and ends the episode with a traceback
The exception is caught and the observation becomes "error: <ExceptionType>: <message>"
The loop retries the same tool call up to three times before giving up on the step
The failing step is removed from history so the policy never sees the failed call
explanation: Errors become observations, not crashes, exactly like a real agent handling a failed command. A crash would end the episode; an observation allows retry.

question: What is the `steps` value in a ReActResult?
options: len(history) - 1, i.e. steps excluding the synthetic task step
len(history), counting the seeded task step as the first step
The number of steps whose observation was an error string
max_steps, always, because the loop records its full step budget
explanation: Because history[0] is the seeded task, the step count subtracts one.

question: Why does run_react take tools as a plain dict[str, callable] instead of importing a tool module?
options: Dependency injection decouples the loop from any one tool set, so it is reusable and testable with tiny tools
Python cannot import a module from inside a function body, so the tools have to be passed in as arguments
A plain dict lookup is much faster than a registry import, which matters because tools run every single step
Tools must be redefined on every step with fresh state, so a statically imported module would go stale
explanation: run_react never imports llmre.tools, so you can drive it with a calculator, filesystem, search API, or test tools. The loop does not care.

question: When run_react exhausts max_steps without a final action, what does it return?
options: It raises RuntimeError with the last observation attached to the error message
The last observation as the answer, with finished=True so callers treat it as done
It restarts the loop from step 0 with max_steps doubled, up to a fixed retry limit
A ReActResult with answer=None and finished=False, a clean, testable halt
explanation: Hitting the budget is a distinct outcome. Real LLM policies sometimes loop forever, so this halt is essential.

question: Where would PyTorch's work happen in a ReAct agent built like run_react?
options: Inside the tools dict, whose entries hold the model's weight tensors between calls
Inside policy(history), where a transformer forward pass yields each Thought and Action
In the history list, which stores the hidden activations of every previous step
In the max_steps check, which runs a small classifier to decide when the loop stops
explanation: The loop has no tensors: an agent is control flow around a policy. Swapping the scripted policy for a model changes nothing about the loop.

section: 5. From a loop to a mini SWE-agent
question: What is the central idea of SWE-agent (Yang et al. 2024)?
options: Coding agents only need a raw shell plus a strong model; any extra interface design is unnecessary overhead
Agents should be trained only on GitHub commit histories so they learn how real developers edit code
The Agent-Computer Interface (commands to view, edit, and run code) matters as much as the model
Test suites should be hidden from coding agents so they cannot overfit their patches to the visible tests
explanation: SWE-agent shows the ACI determines coding-agent performance on real GitHub issues (SWE-bench). A narrow, well-designed interface helps the model reason.

section: 5. From a loop to a mini SWE-agent
question: Why does a narrow, well-designed agent-computer interface beat handing a coding agent a raw shell?
options: Raw shells are too slow for agents, since every command spawns a new process that takes seconds to start
Narrow interfaces let the model skip reading files entirely, because the edit commands infer the context
Raw shells cannot run tests, so the agent never gets pass or fail feedback on its edits without a wrapper
Every command returns a tidy observation, like a clean pass/fail from run_tests, that the model can reason about
explanation: Scoped edits and clean results keep observations interpretable. Raw shell output is noisy and harder to act on.

section: 5. From a loop to a mini SWE-agent
question: What is the course's mini SWE-agent Workspace?
options: An in-memory dict of path -> contents, making the scaffold hermetic and testable
A Docker container with a real filesystem, reset to a clean snapshot after each task
A git repository cloned from GitHub at the commit where the target issue was filed
A tensor of file embeddings that the policy searches to decide which file to open next
explanation: Keeping files in memory means tests never touch disk or network and are fully reproducible.

section: 5. From a loop to a mini SWE-agent
question: Which four tools does the course's mini SWE-agent give the ReAct loop?
options: read_file, write_file, run_tests, and list_files
shell, python, git, and browser, each wrapped as a tool
search, calculator, python_eval, and mock_search
open_file, edit_lines, submit_patch, and find_symbol
explanation: These form the agent-computer interface over the Workspace: inspect, edit, check, and list.

section: 5. From a loop to a mini SWE-agent
question: In the mini SWE-agent, what does run_tests return?
options: The full pytest stdout, including tracebacks for every failure
A bare boolean, True if all tests passed, False otherwise
"PASS: ..." or "FAIL: ..." derived from an injected checker
The number of lines changed since the previous test run
explanation: run_tests formats the injected test_runner's result as a clean PASS/FAIL observation the policy can act on.

section: 5. From a loop to a mini SWE-agent
question: What is solve(policy, workspace, task, test_runner) in the mini SWE-agent?
options: A separate agent loop with its own error handling and step budget
A fine-tuning routine that trains the policy on its successful fixes
Just run_react with file-oriented tools built by make_tools
A planner that writes all of its edits before running any tests
explanation: solve builds the ACI with make_tools(workspace, test_runner) and calls run_react. The same loop becomes a coding agent once its tools are file-oriented.

section: 5. From a loop to a mini SWE-agent
question: What cycle makes the mini SWE-agent an agent rather than a one-shot code generator?
options: read_file (inspect) → write_file (edit) → run_tests (observe) → decide → retry if it failed
Generate the complete patch once from the task description, write it, then stop without testing
Run the tests first, then delete any failing tests from the workspace so the suite reports PASS
List the files repeatedly until one of them changes, then read that file and return its contents
explanation: Inspect-act-observe-correct with retry on failure is the agentic part. A one-shot generator never sees test feedback.

section: 5. From a loop to a mini SWE-agent
question: Why does the course's mini SWE-agent only fix the specific bug its script targets?
options: Because write_file can modify only one file per episode, so multi-file fixes are impossible
Because run_tests checks only one test, so the agent cannot see failures in other parts of the code
Because the Workspace forbids creating new files, so only edits to existing files are possible
Its policy is scripted; a real SWE-agent's LLM policy decides which file to open and what to edit
explanation: The scaffold teaches the interface and loop, not the model. Everything hard about SWE-agent lives in the missing LLM policy.

question: What hardware does the course's ReAct and mini SWE-agent scaffold require?
options: None special: it runs on CPU in well under a second, with no tensors or GPU
A single A100 to run the policy model's forward pass at each loop step
At least 16 GB of GPU memory to hold the history of every step's activations
A multi-node cluster so the four workspace tools can execute in parallel
explanation: The only compute is Python control flow. A real agent's cost is in LLM policy calls, which the scaffold factors out.

question: Where does nearly all the cost of a real LLM agent come from?
options: The Python loop's control flow, which dominates once there are many steps
Appending steps to the history list, which copies the full trace each time
Formatting error strings and observations so the policy can parse them
The LLM policy calls: API latency or GPU inference
explanation: Control flow is negligible. Each policy call is a full model generation.

question: Why do the agent tests in code/tests/test_agents.py define their own add, mul, and noop tools instead of importing llmre.tools?
options: Because llmre.tools has no arithmetic tools, only file and search tools for the SWE scaffold
It shows the decoupling that lets the agents module be built and tested apart from the tools module
Because pytest disallows importing project modules inside a test file that also defines fixtures
Because locally defined tools are compiled and run on the GPU, which makes the test suite faster
explanation: Because run_react takes tools by injection, the tests can use tiny local tools and need nothing from Module 18.

question: Which behaviors do the course's agent tests check?
options: Model accuracy on SWE-bench Verified, per-step latency, and peak GPU memory use during a full agent run on real repositories
Only that every module in llmre.agents imports cleanly without error and exposes each of the documented public functions
The scripted policy solves the arithmetic task in ≤ 3 steps, the loop halts at max_steps, and the SWE scaffold fixes a toy file
That the LLM policy produces identical thoughts across random seeds, so that every agent trace is fully reproducible in CI
explanation: The tests verify the loop mechanics: solving, halting on the budget, and the coding scaffold's fix.

question: With injected sub, add, and mul tools, what is the minimum number of ReAct steps to compute (10 − 3) × (2 + 5)?
options: One step, since the policy can write the whole expression in one call
Two tool-call steps plus a final step, since mul can nest the add call
Three tool-call steps plus a final step
Five steps, one per number, then the operations
explanation: There are three binary operations, each tool returns one value, and mul needs both earlier results. So sub, add, mul, then {"final": 49}.

question: In a scripted ReAct policy computing (10 − 3) × (2 + 5), how does the mul step get the subtraction result?
options: It recomputes 10 − 3 inside the policy without calling a tool
It reads a global variable that the sub tool sets as a side effect
It reaches back into history, e.g. history[1].observation
The mul tool caches previous tool calls and looks up the result
explanation: The running trace is the agent's memory, so earlier observations can be retrieved from history.

question: Why must a ReAct loop treat 'hit the step budget' as a distinct reported outcome rather than success?
options: Because hitting the budget always means a tool crashed and the loop could not recover from the error
It means the policy failed to finish, e.g. looping on the same call, not that the task was solved
Because the last observation at the budget is always the correct answer and must be reported specially
Because the budget is only ever reached on success, when the policy has run every step it planned
explanation: LLM policies sometimes loop forever. Reporting the budget halt separately avoids mistaking non-termination for a result.

question: What is the problem with importing the tool registry into run_react?
options: It makes the loop slower, because the tool module gets loaded twice: once at import and again per call
It causes a circular import in every case, since the tools module itself imports run_react to register
It couples the loop to one tool set, so it can't be tested in isolation or reused with another interface
It prevents the loop from catching tool exceptions, because imported functions raise outside its try block
explanation: Injection keeps the loop generic. Importing tools hard-wires one interface.

question: What is the mistake in 'confusing the scaffold with an agent'?
options: Scaffolds are much slower than agents because they replay every scripted step from the beginning
A deterministic policy is a test harness, not intelligence; the hard part is the LLM that decides
Scaffolds cannot use tools at all, so they only simulate what a real agent's tool calls would return
Agents do not need loops, so any code with a loop is a scaffold rather than a real agent by definition
explanation: The scripted scaffold proves the plumbing works. It doesn't solve unseen tasks.

question: A ReAct policy calls tool 'add' but then checks last.action.get("tool") == "sum" before finalizing. What happens?
options: The loop raises a KeyError on 'sum', since no tool by that name is in the tools dict, and the episode crashes
The check is never true, so the policy keeps calling add(0, 0) and the loop halts at max_steps with answer=None
The policy finalizes after the first add, because get returns None and the comparison falls through to final
The loop finalizes on step 2 with answer 0, because the unknown-tool error string is converted to a zero
explanation: The name mismatch means the final branch is unreachable. Fix by comparing against "add".

question: When a ReAct agent never finalizes, what is the general cause?
options: A tool that returns the wrong type, such as a string where the policy expects an integer result
A max_steps value that is too large, which keeps the loop running long after the answer is known
Almost always a policy that never recognizes the history state in which it should stop
A history list that is truncated too aggressively, so the policy forgets the task before finishing
explanation: The policy branches on history; if no branch matches the stopping state, it never emits final.

question: In the course's run_react, what is appended to history each iteration?
options: Only the observation, since that is the part fed back for the next step
Only the action, so the history is a replayable list of tool calls
The whole Step (thought, action, observation); the policy gets the full history
Nothing; history holds just the task, and the policy reads only the latest step
explanation: The Observation is the part fed back for the next Thought and Action, but the implementation appends the entire Step.

question: Besides testability and reuse, what other benefit does injecting tools into run_react give?
options: It lets tools share one GPU, since injected callables run in the policy's process
It avoids a build-order dependency between modules written in parallel
It encrypts tool arguments in transit, since injected tools never touch disk
It speeds up the policy, because tool lookups are cached between loop steps
explanation: Since the loop doesn't import the tools module, the agents and tools modules can be developed independently.

question: In the mini SWE-agent, what is the signature and role of the injected test_runner?
options: test_runner() -> int, counting the files in the workspace that changed since the episode began
test_runner(policy) -> str, grading the quality of the policy's thoughts with a short written verdict
test_runner(path) -> str, reading one file from the workspace and returning its contents for the policy
test_runner(workspace) -> (passed: bool, message: str), deciding what passing means for the task
explanation: It is injected so the scaffold never hard-codes correctness; each task supplies its checker, like different repos have different test suites. run_tests formats its result as PASS/FAIL.

question: After building agents, what does the course name as the final piece of the research-engineer toolkit?
options: Designing experiments, measuring honestly across seeds, and writing up findings reproducibly
Writing custom CUDA and Triton kernels for every agent tool so that policy calls run faster
Training a larger tokenizer on agent traces so that tool calls compress into fewer tokens
Deploying agents to production clusters with autoscaling, monitoring, and on-call rotations
explanation: The last piece isn't code: it is experiment design, multi-seed measurement, and trustworthy write-ups.
